A tradition attributed to the tenth Shiite Imam, ’Alî-Naqî, says that beyond the encircling Sphere of Spheres—that is, beyond Mount Qâf—God possesses a green Emerald whose colour is reflected throughout the sky. But we are not speaking here of optical perception: what matters is the meaning of colours as expressions of different levels of being. Green marks the world of the Malakût, the world closest to ours, whose proper colour is black, or “black light” (nûr-e siyâh). This visio smaragdina, this emerald vision, is the Malakût: the universe of the Soul with its seventy thousand worlds , the “heavenly Earth with its cities of emerald” (Jâbalqâ, Jâbarsâ, Hûrqalyâ). According to some traditions, all of Mount Qâf is made of emerald. But there is an underlying parallel here, similar to the one Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î explicitly draws between the formation of the “resurrection body” and the alchemical Operation . Around the turn of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the masters of the revival of Iranian Sufism, Nur ’Ali-Shah and Mozaffar ’Ali-Shah, likewise described the successive stages of mystical union (unio mystica) in alchemical terms .

I. Who is the personal Angel? Anyone who has read, and perhaps carefully reflected upon, this tale by Suhrawardī will gradually have recognised and confirmed all the themes we examined at the beginning of this chapter as making up the “history of the gnostic.” The theme of the self as an “objective reality” involved in self-knowledge—in the act by which the knowing subject comes to know himself—has found its final resolution, in the musical sense of the word, in the encounter with the Angel on the mystical Sinai.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01538

More precisely, the self now appears to us as our essential, authentic “I,” but as an “I” addressed as you: an alter ego so real that the earthly “I,” its reflection and exiled image, can enter into dialogue with it. That it is the gnostic's eternal archetype; that it reveals his origin and what he was before being manifested, projected and exiled into this world; that, in order to find it again and be reunited with it, the gnostic must undertake the search for self-knowledge whose stages Suhrawardī has just shown us, all the way to the passage through the Spring of Life—all this is attested by the Angel's declarations to the gnostic who is its “child,” just as the Angel itself is the “child” of the Angel before it.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01539

The names most characteristic of this being in Islamic gnosis are equivalents of those used for the Angel in gnosis more generally : the essential or real human being (al-insān al-ḥaqīqī—ho ontōs anthrōpos), the Perfect Human Being (al-insān al-kāmil—anthrōpos teleios), Perfect Nature, the luminous self, the human being of light (shakhs nūrānī), and so on. We have already noted the close affinity between the form of light that unites with the Ismaili initiate and the luminous self of Manichaean gnosis .

In short, through many different approaches and variations, we are brought back to a conception of the Angel very close to the angelos of Valentinian gnosis: the Angel of which “we are a portion.” Similarly, in the “Tale of the Exile,” the Angel on Sinai contains the gnostic, who is its child, and is itself contained within the Angel before it. As the gnostic's heavenly counterpart, the Angel expresses his whole being, his being in its fullness—his pleroma.
